Lessons.Title: Area Situations
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve original information-gap rectangular-area problems by asking an informed partner for the necessary relationships, and solve optional whole-number-by-fraction missing-factor equations. The communication protocol is essential; a single given dimension is not automatically sufficient.
Warm-up — Number Talk: calculate 3×(10÷2)=15, (3/2)×10=15, (14/7)×10=20, and 14×(10/7)=20. Explain why dividing first by seven makes the last product manageable without changing the whole.

Activity 1 — Info Gap: Area source cards: one learner has a problem card, another has a private data card and must not show it. Learners work on two cases, switch roles, and may need successive questions to obtain a relationship between sides rather than being directly handed the missing width. Teacher narrative mentions a paper towel and a corn field, but the actual original card dimensions have NOT been inspected. Do not claim the previous first-party 4×7 1/2 art-panel or 15 3/4÷3 examples are original publisher cards. Use those transparently as additional Edulytiks practice while preserving the essential ask/explain/revise/derive protocol.

Activity 2 — OPTIONAL Fill in the Blank from public Student Facing teacher lesson: 1/3×18=6; (7/9)×3=21/9; (1/15)×30=2; 9×6 2/3=60; 14 99/100×10=149 9/10; 7 3/5×6=45 3/5; and 4×6 9/10=27 3/5. Learners must identify whether the missing value is a factor or product and explain equivalent grouping.

Teacher/source boundary: source HTML verifies warm-up, info-gap procedure and all seven optional equations; original card blackline master, exact publisher figures, separate Student Task PDF, teacher responses and protected Cool-down remain NOT_VERIFIED. Teacher checks the learner's actual questions, data-relationship reasoning and role-switch dialogue; arithmetic alone is not completion.

KeyConcepts.Title: Information required for area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A rectangle's area depends on two perpendicular side lengths.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If only one side is known and area is unknown, ask for the other side or equivalent missing information.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four feet by an undisclosed width has no unique area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole by mixed-number area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive whole-number side can multiply a whole-plus-fraction side.

KeyConcepts.Title: Missing side from area
KeyConcepts.Definition: An unknown length can be derived by dividing area by known perpendicular length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: width = area ÷ height, with square feet ÷ feet = feet.

WorkedExamples.Title: Info Gap source protocol: no unverified original numbers
WorkedExamples.Question: A student has a rectangular area question without the width; a partner holds relational data, not necessarily the width itself. How should the student proceed?
WorkedExamples.Method: Describe the source's real inquiry flow before computing any chosen first-party numeric example.
Steps: Identify that both perpendicular lengths or equivalent length relationship and one dimension are needed.
Ask the data-card holder what relation or dimension they know and why it matters.
Use the relationship to infer the missing side, then compute area and square units.
Repeat with roles reversed on the second card; teacher checks precision of questions and responses.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Request the missing relationship and justify it before calculating; no uniquely published width can be claimed without inspecting the original card.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original source teacher HTML describes a paper towel/corn field and partner data card, not the invented first-party art panel dimensions.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party extension only: 4×7 1/2 art panel (NOT source info-gap card)
WorkedExamples.Question: The art panel is 4 feet high and its partner reports a width of 7 1/2 feet. Find its area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason from the exact contextual quantities with an original diagram, estimate and equation.
Steps: Decompose width into 7 feet plus 1/2 foot.
Compute 4×7=28 square feet and 4×1/2=2 square feet.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party extension only: infer 5 1/4 from 15 3/4÷3
WorkedExamples.Question: A panel has area 15 3/4 square feet and height 3 feet. Find its width.
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason from the exact contextual quantities with an original diagram, estimate and equation.
Steps: Convert area to 63/4 square feet and divide by 3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original OPTIONAL Fill in the Blank sample — missing factor and mixed products
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve source equations 7/9×?=21/9 and 1/15×?=2; also find 9×6 2/3.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use a common nonzero denominator and inverse multiplication before evaluating mixed-number products.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The area varies when the undisclosed side changes; guessing falsely suggests a unique result.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Ask for the missing width, or explicitly state assumptions before producing an estimate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Report square feet for a side length
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The result of area divided by a length has linear units, not square units.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep the unit on every quantity and cancel area units against the known side length.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Present invented art-panel dimensions as the original Info Gap: Area blackline cards
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Public source HTML documents the protocol, paper towel and corn field, not the unavailable card measurements or an automatic exact-width disclosure.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label Edulytiks art-panel values FIRST_PARTY_EXTENSION; preserve source's progressive question/data relationship and role switch, with human assessment.

SummaryPoints: Original warm-up gives 15,15,20,20 by explaining equivalent division/multiplication.
Info Gap: Area requires a concealed partner data card, missing relationship, precise follow-up questions and role switch; uninspected card numbers are NOT published source facts.
Optional source Fill in the Blank uses seven equations with missing factors and fraction/mixed-number products; student should justify the solution.
Source evidence: 2021 public teacher lesson/preparation Student Facing HTML; blackline master, Student Task PDF and gated content NOT_VERIFIED.

Lessons.Title: Multiply More Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use the original source's six-number bank EXACTLY ONCE across three related real-world area situations; then match four equivalent expressions and diagrams for 4×5 2/3. The existing unrelated first-party panel bank may be used only as an extension, not substituted for the source task.

Warm-up — original four number-talk products: 6×3/8=18/8=2 1/4; 6×2 3/8=14 1/4; 7×9/10=6 3/10; 7×3 9/10=27 3/10. Explain the jump from fraction-only to mixed-number multiplication and compensation by subtracting 7×1/10 from 7×4.

Activity 1 — Multiply Your Way: source number bank 4, 5, 5 1/2, 3, 5 3/4, 2, each used exactly once. A 16 1/2-square-foot rug has sides 3 and 5 1/2 feet; a puzzle is 2 1/2 feet wide, 2 feet long, area 5 square feet; a 23-square-foot whiteboard has side lengths 4 and 5 3/4 feet. These six choices solve the same linked puzzle and must preserve feet versus square feet.

Activity 2 — Equivalent Expressions: match source diagrams A-D to the same quantity 4×5 2/3=4×17/3=68/3=22 2/3 square units. The four original expressions are (4×5)+(4×2/3), (4×6)−(4×1/3), 4×17/3, and (4×17)÷3. Explain every valid geometry-based grouping; the different diagrams express the same total, not necessarily the same physical subdivision.

Teacher/source boundary: partner revision, the six-number use-once rule, unit classification and actual diagram-to-expression explanation require teacher review. Public original teacher lesson/preparation and embedded Student Facing HTML compared, but separate Student Task PDF/individual visual rights and protected Cool-down NOT_VERIFIED. Prior first-party 18/13/27 panel exercise is a supplemental option only.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use-once constrained assignments
KeyConcepts.Definition: A collection of candidate side lengths may be assigned to multiple area equations without repeating entries.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Check every target area and track each candidate number's usage exactly once.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distributive mixed-number products
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplication by a mixed number decomposes into whole and fractional products.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compensation near a whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mixed number close to the next whole can be multiplied by that whole minus a small fraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original six-number use-once bank
WorkedExamples.Question: Use 4, 5, 5 1/2, 3, 5 3/4, 2 exactly once to complete rug 16 1/2 ft², puzzle width 2 1/2 ft, whiteboard 23 ft².
WorkedExamples.Method: Constrain the area products and each available slot; check all six bank values are consumed once.
Steps: Puzzle length 2 ft with fixed width 2 1/2 ft, so area=5 ft²; the bank contributes 2 and 5.
Whiteboard side lengths 4 ft and 5 3/4 ft, giving 23 ft².
Confirm 3,5 1/2,2,5,4,5 3/4 each appears once and every linear/area unit is correct.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Rug: 3 ft, 5 1/2 ft; puzzle: 2-ft length, 5-ft² area; whiteboard: 4 ft, 5 3/4 ft.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Equivalent Expressions — 4×5 2/3
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate the original product using four source expressions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use addition, subtract from six, improper thirds, or divide integer product by three.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 68/3=22 2/3 square units, in all four cases.
WorkedExamples.Check: The expression corresponds to four unit-height rows across five and two-thirds units.

WorkedExamples.Title: First-party extension only: 7×3 9/10 compensation (source warm-up)
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 7×3 9/10 exactly.
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason from the exact contextual quantities with an original diagram, estimate and equation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reuse a side length across two separate panels
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source's linked constraints allocate each given number only once, so locally correct products can still be an invalid overall solution.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Track all candidate lengths and check the complete assignment globally.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The distributive property multiplies the fractional difference by the outside factor.

SummaryPoints: Original constrained bank uses six values 4,5,5 1/2,3,5 3/4,2 exactly once for rug, puzzle and whiteboard (area 16 1/2,5,23).
Original 4×5 2/3=68/3 can be shown by four distinct source equations, and source diagrams A–D need teacher-scored correspondence.
Fractional dimensions are feet; resulting area is square feet. Review each learner's revisions and justification.
Source compared: 2021 first-edition teacher lesson/preparation Student Facing. Original PDF, source image rights, protected Cool-down NOT_VERIFIED.

Lessons.Title: Estimate Products (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: estimate whole-number by mixed-number products, using the source's actual garden with 36-square-foot material limit, then estimate two specific large products and form a value close to 20. This OPTIONAL lesson values magnitude justification more than a fixed result without stated conditions.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: the source presents an unlabeled garden image and asks which lengths could make an area between 30 and 40 square feet. For example 8×4=32, 7×5=35, or 10×3 1/8=31 1/4; explain why a length near 3–4 with a suitable partner dimension can fit the interval. No original photograph is reproduced.

Activity 1 — Priya's Garden: source target is 36 square feet. Four candidates: A 9×4 2/3=42 square feet (exceeds 36); B 9×3 8/9=35 square feet (one below target); C 12×2 11/12=35 square feet (one below target); D 9×2 2/3=24 square feet (far below target). Under a strict material upper bound B,C,D are within budget; if the task's 'reasonable for her 36-square-foot garden' means close to full use, B and C are the two plausible near-target choices, while D may be too small. Do NOT silently treat all within-budget values as equally reasonable or invent a unique publisher rubric; teacher scores the interpretation and argument.

Activity 2 — Too High, Too Low, Just About Right: bound 7×12 8/9 = 90 2/9 between 7×12=84 and 7×13=91; estimate 9×4 2/29 = 36 18/29 between 9×4=36 and 37. Explain an integer product just below, just above, and close to each exact value (several answers may be valid). Use digits 2,3,5,6,7 to build a product near 20, e.g. 6×3 2/5=20 2/5 as a nonunique first-party example; justify the magnitude instead of grading one expression as the only answer.

Teacher/source limitations: source images, original Student Task PDF, answer key and gated Cool-down not verified; open estimate bounds and student's use of 'reasonable' require teacher evaluation. A solely numeric chosen-set grade could incorrectly accept a far-under-budget 24 ft² as the intended 36 ft² garden.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number product bounds
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mixed factor lies between neighboring whole numbers, giving bounds for its positive product.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If n<m+f<n+1 and a>0, then an<a(n+f)<a(n+1).

KeyConcepts.Title: Area budget inequality
KeyConcepts.Definition: A proposed rectangle fits only when its computed area is no larger than the allowed maximum.

KeyConcepts.Title: Compensation for a near-whole factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Subtracting the small missing fraction may be easier than direct mixed multiplication.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Priya's 36-square-foot garden choices
WorkedExamples.Question: Evaluate source candidate areas 9×4 2/3, 9×3 8/9, 12×2 11/12 and 9×2 2/3; which approximate 36 square feet?
WorkedExamples.Method: Use benchmark 9×4=36 and 12×3=36; compare size and justify closeness.
Steps: A=9×(14/3)=42, too big for a 36-square-foot material limit.
D=9×(8/3)=24, below the limit but much smaller than 36; distinguish budget-eligible from close-to-target.
WorkedExamples.Answer: B and C are close to target at 35 ft² each; A is 42 ft², and D is only 24 ft². Teacher judges whether D is 'reasonable' under the intended condition.
WorkedExamples.Check: No unsupported definitive source answer for ambiguous 'reasonable'; if criterion means strictly ≤36, then B, C and D are within budget.

WorkedExamples.Title: Bound two source products without rounding away fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: Estimate 7×12 8/9 and 9×4 2/29.
WorkedExamples.Method: Bound the mixed side and compute exact results as an independent check.
Steps: Choose an integer product near each result and explain whether it lies above or below.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 90 2/9 and 36 18/29; multiple whole-number products may be defensible estimates.

WorkedExamples.Title: Illustrative digit-choice expression near 20
WorkedExamples.Question: Use source digits 2,3,5,6,7 to build a whole number times mixed number with a value near 20. Give one defensible example.
WorkedExamples.Method: Choose a leading product near 20 and add a small fraction, not an arbitrary unique answer.
Steps: Choose six as whole factor and three as mixed-number whole part: base=18.
Use two fifths as fractional part, making mixed number 3 2/5.
WorkedExamples.Answer: One illustrative choice is 6×3 2/5=20 2/5 (20.4), with several other solutions possible.
WorkedExamples.Check: Digits used are from the supplied list; teacher confirms how source asks pupils to allocate the digits.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reject a garden exactly equal to the budget
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An upper bound stated as 'at most' allows equality.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Include candidate rectangles whose areas equal, as well as fall below, the limit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignore the fractional part when estimating too close to an upper bound
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A small positive fractional strip may push the total over the allowable area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Estimate the fractional correction and compare the full product with the threshold.

SummaryPoints: Source Priya garden target is 36 ft², NOT 30. A=42, B=35, C=35, D=24 ft²; distinguish budget ceiling from close-to-target 'reasonable' choice.
Source estimation includes 7×12 8/9=90 2/9 and 9×4 2/29=36 18/29 and constructing a product near 20 from digit choices.
Initial estimates and teacher-approved reasoning matter: multiple number products and 'reasonable' justifications are possible.
Public 2021 teacher lesson/preparation Student Facing HTML compared. Publisher figures, original Student Task PDF, protected Cool-down and original rubric NOT_VERIFIED.

Lessons.Title: Mosaic Pictures (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: OPTIONAL hands-on collaborative mosaic design with identical paper rectangles where one side is a whole number and the other a mixed length greater than one; justify each piece's square-unit area and estimate MATERIAL COST for the combined design.

Warm-up — Notice and Wonder: examine source mosaic butterfly attributed to Gordon Johnson/Pixabay and discuss different component shapes, pattern and unit measurement. Source photograph is not reproduced; each student group must share one measurement unit (inches or centimeters) before cutting paper.

Activity 1 — Create a Mosaic: each member of a group cuts identical rectangles from colored paper, choosing a positive whole-number side and a fraction-greater-than-one side; use a ruler and paper, verify the per-rectangle area with an expression, then collectively arrange selected pieces to make a mosaic on poster paper. An independently authored example is a 3-inch by 1 1/2-inch piece, area 4 1/2 in²; 4 nonoverlapping pieces cover 18 in². Students do NOT need to use all pieces and there is no one correct design.

Activity 2 — Cost of Mosaic (previous candidate omission): the original source asks the approximate cost for the group's chosen mosaic using the provided materials table: stone $5 per square unit, tile $3 per square unit, glass $2 per square unit. For a first-party four-tile, non-overlapping 18-square-unit mosaic, stone costs $90, tile $54 and glass $36; learners choose a preferred material, estimate appropriate total covered area and explain the bill, including partial pieces and units as necessary. Actual source learner mosaic dimensions are open, so no one fixed price is mandatory.

Teacher/source boundaries: teacher checks physical cut dimensions and same unit, selected-pieces/no-overlap area, materials and cost expressions, group reasoning and revised peer explanation. Original source Student Task PDF, butterfly asset rights, individual source figures and gated response NOT_VERIFIED. Neither source mosaic image nor unique classroom outcome is fabricated.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed fractional side of a mosaic tile
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each identical rectangular tile has a positive whole-number side and a mixed-number side greater than one.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Area = whole side × mixed side in squared units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Congruent pieces and consistent units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Identical mosaic tiles share dimensions and area, even if rotated.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep inches with inches or centimeters with centimeters; report square inches or square centimeters.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four identical 4 1/2-square-inch pieces cover 18 square inches without overlap.

KeyConcepts.Title: Layout versus covered area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Arranging tiles in a new pattern can change the shape of a mosaic without changing the area of the same nonoverlapping pieces.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For n disjoint congruent pieces of area A, total covered area is n×A.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit-cost scaling for mosaics
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mosaic's material cost depends on the measured total covered area and a chosen price per square unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Estimated cost = area in square units × dollars per square unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: An 18-in² mosaic costs $36 using a $2-per-square-unit glass material.

WorkedExamples.Title: Area of one colored tile
WorkedExamples.Question: A mosaic tile measures 3 inches by 1 1/2 inches. What is its area?
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason from the exact contextual quantities with an original diagram, estimate and equation.
Steps: Split the width into one inch plus half an inch.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source-based first-party example: four selected rectangles
WorkedExamples.Question: Four nonoverlapping 3×1 1/2-inch rectangles are assembled into a mosaic. What surface area is covered?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply the area of each identical piece by the number actually used.
Steps: Four selected pieces cover 4×4 1/2=18 square inches.
A source learner's open design could use another count; the four-piece setup is Edulytiks-authored.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 18 square inches in this illustrative four-piece configuration.
WorkedExamples.Check: If pieces overlap, area covered requires subtracting overlap; if unused, count only included pieces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Cost of Mosaic — first-party worked pricing example
WorkedExamples.Question: Suppose the selected tiles cover 18 square units. Estimate cost with stone $5, tile $3, or glass $2 per square unit.
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply covered square units by chosen price per square unit.
Steps: Name the chosen material, the number of used square units and a defensible approximate total.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Stone $90, tile $54, or glass $36 for the illustrative 18-square-unit mosaic.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original task gives unit prices but actual student design's area can vary; a teacher checks dimensions and material choice.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Measure mosaic pieces in mismatched units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A product of inches by centimeters is not directly a square-inch or square-centimeter area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose one unit system for the group and use it consistently.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Count unused or overlapping pieces as fully covered mosaic area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Only the selected, nonoverlapping regions cover distinct area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: List included pieces, account for overlaps and let the teacher inspect the assembled work.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignore the original cost-of-mosaic task or fix one universal final price
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source's second activity includes three material costs and an open design whose area depends on selected rectangles and placement.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use source $5/$3/$2 price table with student-chosen area and chosen material, record supporting units and teacher-check the constructed design.

SummaryPoints: Students create a mosaic by cutting congruent colored paper rectangles, with one whole-number side and one mixed-number side above one, using a shared unit.
Source's second activity asks approximate cost per square unit: stone $5, tile $3, glass $2. Multiply actual chosen mosaic area by selected rate.
For illustration only, four 3×1 1/2-inch tiles cover 18 in² and cost $90/$54/$36 for stone/tile/glass respectively.
No fixed learner art/design/cost is assumed. Physical work, photographs, source figure rights and protected Cool-down not verified.
